sources.note: No phonology content: the entry gives only location ('dituturkan di Kampung Yarona.. dengan jumlah penutur sekitar 275 jiwa'), the claim that surrounding villages speak the same language, Asmat-Kamoro affiliation (in the blog-quoted print version), and dialectometric distances (Kamberau 96.5%, Baham 99.25%, Kowiai 99.5%). sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1975. Languages of Irian Jaya: Checklist. Preliminary classification, language maps, wordlists. Pacific Linguistics B-31. Canberra: Australian National University. (entry 39 'Asienara (Karufa, Buruwai)', p.32; Appendix comparative wordlist col. 39 'Asienara (Ae)')
sources.note: No phonology content. The Appendix 'A note on the orthography' explains that all lists were respelled in a unified comparative orthography 'which is neither phonemic nor accurately phonetic'; no stress or tone marks are carried. Asienara column: mada 'arm', umida 'ashes', dea 'bird', akara 'black', eta 'blood', ekera 'bone', nawara 'come', iwura 'dog', nara 'eat', asara 'egg', marada 'eye', fetakera 'fingernail', usara 'fire', morami 'give', mareda 'good', seta 'ground', fida 'hair', yabida 'head', noda 'I', mavura 'leg', buekera 'louse', bevura 'man', ura 'name', iweta 'night', sasiawara 'on…

sources.note: Historical-phonology tables reproduce Walker (& Hesse 1988) pre-phonemic survey forms for S. Kamrau (Yarona) with stress marks on individual words; no rule stated. My script tally of that column (check observation, not a published claim): 96 stress-marked polysyllabic forms, 90 marked on the first syllable, 6 on the second.
